title: LCA-PINN: A lightweight condition-aware physics-informed neural network for interpretable tool wear monitoring
Physics-informed unit-normalized selective embedding with harmonic loss for fault identification using vibration and acoustic signals
abstract: Induction motors generate vibration and acoustic signals from mechanical imbalance, electromagnetic forces, and structural transmission through the machine housing. Interpreting harmonic fault signatures from these responses becomes difficult when different types of sensors are used due to bandwidth and signal scaling limitations. This work investigates how physics-informed signal representation can improve fault diagnosis using both industrial sensors and cell phone sensors. A unit-consistent normalization approach is introduced to allow comparison between vibration acceleration and acoustic pressure signals by converting both signals into equivalent vibration velocity representations. Based on this formulation, a structured signal processing framework named Unit-Normalized Selective Embedding with Harmonic Loss (UNSE-HL) is proposed, combining unit normalization, selective embedding, and a physics-informed harmonic loss function to improve the representation of modulation patterns during diagnosis. Experiments are conducted using the induction motor datasets collected under multiple operating conditions with both structurally mounted sensors and cell phones. Envelope spectral analysis shows that rotor harmonics are observable across cell phone sensors after normalization; this observability does not by itself establish classification reliability, which is evaluated separately. Time-frequency representations combined with the proposed embedding strategy improve diagnosis accuracy and classification stability relative to conventional signal representation approaches on the datasets and devices evaluated in this study. These findings highlight the importance of signal transmission physics in condition monitoring and indicate that, for the specific smartphone sensors and operating conditions tested here, appropriate preprocessing improves the usability of low-bandwidth sensors for fault diagnosis.

title: Causal Bayesian optimization for sensor placement and deconfounding in structural health monitoring
Early anomaly detection in wind Turbines by Causality-based graph attention networks
abstract: Early anomaly detection is a key issue for ensuring reliability, availability and efficiency in Wind Turbines (WTs) operation. Traditional condition monitoring techniques struggle to identify anomalies because of: i) the strong interconnections among the subsystems of a WT, which induce complex spatio-temporal dependencies in the measured signals and can enable the cascading propagation of the effects of anomalies, ii) the variability of the operating conditions, which can affect the anomaly signatures, and iii) the presence of control systems that can mask the anomalies signatures. To address these challenges, this work proposes a novel anomaly detection method employing a Graph Neural Network (GNN) autoencoder. GNN is selected for its capability in modeling the interconnected nature of subsystems and capturing the spatio-temporal dependencies in operational signals. A key contribution is the use of the Granger causality test to generate the GNN functional graph. By leveraging the causal relationships among turbine signals, the obtained graph ensures that the learned topology reflects the underlying physical dependencies rather than spurious correlations, as it may occur in traditional graphs. To handle variability of the operating conditions, graph attention layers adaptively weight sensor relationships, while gated recurrent units process the temporal dynamics. The proposed method is validated on synthetic data simulated using a high-fidelity WT model and applied to SCADA data collected from real WTs. Results demonstrate a 4% increase in recall and a 45% reduction in detection delay compared to state-of-the-art methods.

title: An integrated autoencoder-based framework for unsupervised domain adaptation in structural health monitoring of bridges
abstract: The limited availability of long-term bridge-monitoring data presents a significant obstacle to the application of machine learning in structural health monitoring (SHM). Domain adaptation offers a means of addressing this data scarcity, but existing methods often have limited generalization and are sensitive to hyperparameter choices. This study proposes a reconstruction-based domain adaptation framework in which target-domain observations are geometrically aligned with the latent space learned by an autoencoder trained on data from a source bridge and, subsequently, reconstructed using its decoder. Unlike conventional feature-alignment approaches, the proposed formulation transfers the reconstruction model itself, enabling target-domain evaluation without labels, classifier retraining, or threshold recalibration. The autoencoder is trained on baseline data collected during commissioning of the source bridge, using observations composed of natural frequencies as damage-sensitive features. Adaptation is performed through orthogonal Procrustes alignment in the latent space, followed by reconstruction with the source-trained decoder. Validation using the Z24 Bridge dataset demonstrates that the framework mitigates seasonal domain shift while preserving sensitivity to controlled damage. The approach is then transferred to a twin bridge over the Itacaiúnas River using only latent-space alignment and no model retraining. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework enables damage assessment across bridges while substantially reducing the data and training requirements for practical deployment.

title: Deep reinforcement learning for semi-active structural control using a variable inerter device
abstract: Structural control devices employing inerters have attracted considerable attention owing to their superior vibration mitigation performance. Variable inerter devices, which enable real-time adjustment of inertance and damping, offer further performance enhancement but also introduce a challenging nonlinear control problem. This paper proposes a deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based control strategy for a tuned variable inertial mass electromagnetic transducer (TVIMET) installed in a five-story base-isolated building. The proposed controller is developed using recurrent proximal policy optimization (RPPO) with long short-term memory (LSTM) networks to account for both the partially observable nature of practical structural control and the history-dependent nonlinear behavior of the lead–rubber bearing (LRB) isolation system. Numerical simulations are conducted under a wide range of earthquake excitations, and the proposed method is compared with passive base isolation, a passive tuned viscous mass damper (TVMD), and a semi-active tuned inertial mass electromagnetic transducer (TIMET). The proposed TVIMET successfully adapts both the inertance and damping coefficient according to the changing dynamic characteristics of the structure. Unlike the passive TVMD, which is designed assuming post-yield structural behavior, the proposed controller remains effective even under earthquake excitations that do not induce significant yielding of the isolation layer. It also achieves the best overall vibration reduction, particularly in terms of the RMS structural responses. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of simultaneously adapting the inertance and damping through DRL for nonlinear structural vibration control.

title: FNO-PD: A Fourier neural operator-based physics-based data-driven framework for efficient dynamic response computation in vehicle-track coupled systems
Physics-informed identification of dynamic propeller excitations via EM-based Kalman filtering
Physics-informed DeepONet with modal coordinate encoding for predicting dynamic responses of unseen motor housings
